# Rocketwind — Tailwind-style CSS, generated by Go

If your Go app lets people build pages or edit their theme, the CSS you need
doesn't exist when you build the app. It depends on what someone saves tomorrow.

Rocketwind is being built to compile that CSS inside your Go process. No Node
process, no build step for each edit, and no need to ship every possible utility
class to every visitor.

**Work in progress.** Core utilities, variants, stylesheet directives and the
Go plugin API work, along with typed settings, named classes, forms and
typography and the other standard plugins. The CLI and compatibility profiles
are still being built.
See [WORK.md](WORK.md) for the implementation gates.


Why?
----

Three things that are awkward with a conventional CSS build:

* **Generate CSS on the fly.** A template, page builder or plugin introduces
  `grid-cols-3` after your binary has shipped. Compile what it uses when you load
  the template, and cache the result.
* **Give each account its own CSS.** Different organizations choose different
  colors, fonts, spacing and components. Compile a stylesheet for each account
  from its configuration, without rebuilding your application.
* **Let people edit settings.** A theme editor stores a heading size and a brand
  color. A component can say `text-{heading.size} bg-{brand.color}`. Your code
  supplies the values and their types; Rocketwind turns them into CSS for a
  named class such as `.signup-button`.

The last case matters because Tailwind's names can be ambiguous. `text-*` can
mean a font size or a color. A setting's type should settle that question even
when its value is a CSS variable. Rocketwind does not guess from its name.

Ordinary helper classes work too: pass in `text-xl`, `hover:flex` and the other
classes your templates use, and get a stylesheet back. Configuration can come
from Go; you don't need a single entry-point CSS file.

```go
compiler := rocketwind.New(rocketwind.Config{
    Theme: map[string]string{"--color-brand": "#663399"},
})
css, err := compiler.Build([]string{"grid", "p-4", "text-xl", "bg-brand"})
```

Or start with a stylesheet containing `@theme`, `@utility`, `@apply` and
`@tailwind utilities`, using `rocketwind.Compile(css, config)`. Imports can use
`Config.LoadStylesheet`; Go configuration and plugins use `Config.LoadModule`.
The standard Tailwind theme and preflight stylesheet are built in.

For configuration entirely in Go, `NewWithPlugins(config, plugins...)` runs
plugin callbacks before returning the compiler. `PluginAPI` registers base
styles, component selectors, static utilities, variants and typed functional
utilities with named values, fractions, modifiers and negative values.

Existing object-style Tailwind configuration has a Go equivalent too:

```go
compiler, err := rocketwind.NewWithPlugins(rocketwind.Config{},
    rocketwind.Legacy(rocketwind.ConfigObject{
        {Key: "theme", Value: map[string]any{
            "extend": map[string]any{
                "colors": map[string]string{"brand": "#663399"},
            },
        }},
    }),
)
```

`Legacy` supports theme replacements and extensions, presets, typed Go theme
callbacks, breakpoints, container settings, dark mode, prefixes and blocklists.
Use `ConfigObject` when field order matters, or ordinary maps for nested values.
`ThemeFunc` receives a resolver for references to other settings. Plugin callbacks
can read scalar values with `Theme`, or objects and tuples with `ThemeValue`.
This is Tailwind 4's compatibility API; it does not yet reproduce Tailwind 3's
generated CSS.

`compiler.Parse(class)` exposes the parsed candidates, including explicit value
types. `compiler.Print(candidate)` produces their normalized spelling.

`Build` compiles exactly the classes passed to it; separate accounts do not
accumulate each other's classes. For a file watcher or a growing template set,
use `compiler.NewBuilder()`. Its `Build` method accumulates candidates, compiles
only additions, and returns cached CSS when nothing changed. `Reset` starts a
fresh stylesheet. Compilers and prepared templates can be shared across
goroutines; each incremental builder belongs to one caller.


Editable settings and named classes
----------------------------------

Prepare a class list once. Supply types now and values when an account's CSS is
needed:

```go
settings := map[string]rocketwind.ValueType{
    "heading.size": rocketwind.TypeLength,
    "brand.color":  rocketwind.TypeColor,
}
button, err := compiler.Prepare("text-{heading.size} bg-{brand.color}",
    rocketwind.TemplateOptions{
        TypeOf: func(name string) (rocketwind.ValueType, error) {
            return settings[name], nil
        },
    })
css, err = button.CSS(".signup-button", func(p rocketwind.Parameter) (rocketwind.Value, error) {
    return rocketwind.Value{CSS: accountSettings[p.Expression]}, nil
})
```

Rocketwind treats expressions such as `heading.size` as opaque strings. Your code
owns lookup, inheritance and validation. Values are literal CSS: underscores and
spaces are preserved. Set `Named: true` to supply a theme token such as `xl`
instead, or `Omit: true` to leave out a utility whose setting is unset.

A whole-class parameter, such as `hover:{button.styles}`, has type `TypeClasses`.
Return `Value{Classes: anotherTemplate}` to inline it. Its `Resolve` field can
supply a different resolver, preserving the scope where those classes were
defined. References inherit surrounding variants and `!`; cycles are errors.
Parameters also work inside arbitrary values and variants, for example
`w-[calc(100%_-_{gap})]` and `min-{breakpoint}:flex`.

Use `compiler.Render([]rocketwind.Rule{...})` to compile several named selectors
with one set of shared theme variables and property registrations. Named rules
preserve class-list order, so later declarations can override earlier ones.
Prepared templates can be reused concurrently with independent resolvers.

Older class spellings can opt into `Config.Aliases`. For example,
`"family": {Utility: "font", Type: rocketwind.TypeFamilyName}` makes `family-*`
mean a font family. Aliases do not change the default Tailwind vocabulary.
`TemplateOptions.DollarReferences` also accepts `$name` as shorthand for `{name}`.


Extract classes from templates
------------------------------

```go
source := rocketwind.Preprocess(template, "vue")
css, err := compiler.Build(rocketwind.Candidates(source))
```

`Candidates` recognizes complete class names and CSS variable references in
source text. It follows Tailwind's scanner; it does not execute template code
or join fragments such as `"text-" + color`. Your template must contain the full
class name, or your application must supply it to the compiler.

`Preprocess` handles Tailwind's supported template languages, including Vue,
Svelte, Pug, Haml, Slim, Ruby, Rust, Clojure and Elixir. Plain HTML, GoX and
unrecognized file extensions pass through unchanged. Processing preserves byte
offsets. `Extract` returns tokens with their source offsets; `AppendExtracted`
reuses a caller-owned buffer without allocating. `CSSVariables` extracts only
`var(...)` references from CSS.

For files on disk, a scanner applies the stylesheet's `@source` directives,
automatic source root and ignore rules:

```go
scanner := compiler.NewScanner(projectDirectory)
css, err := compiler.Build(scanner.Scan())
```

Use `NewScanner([]rocketwind.Source{...})` to supply sources directly. The scanner
follows symlinks, respects `.gitignore` and `.ignore`, and skips binary files and
common generated directories. Explicit sources can include otherwise ignored
files. CSS files contribute variable references, rather than class definitions.

Keep a scanner with an incremental builder for watch mode. `Scan` returns all
candidates found so far; `ScanContent` returns additions from supplied files or
text. Removed candidates remain until you create a new scanner, as in Tailwind.
`Files`, `Globs` and `ScannedFiles` expose watch inputs and the files read by the
last scan. Each scanner belongs to one build session; do not share it between
concurrent builds or accounts.


Command-line compiler
---------------------

```sh
go install github.com/andreyvit/rocketwind/cmd/rocketwind@latest
rocketwind -i src/input.css -o public/app.css
rocketwind -i src/input.css -o public/app.css --watch
```

The CLI reads files or stdin (`-i -`), writes files or stdout (`-o -`), and uses
Tailwind's automatic source discovery and `@source` directives. Without an input
file, it compiles `@import "tailwindcss"`. Use `--cwd` to choose the search root,
`--content` for explicit source patterns, and `--classes` for extra class names.

Use `--exclude public/admin.css` to generate only helpers absent from an existing
stylesheet. Both `--content` and `--exclude` can be repeated.

`--config theme.json` loads Tailwind's object-style configuration. JSON `plugins`
can list the built-in plugin names, such as `"@tailwindcss/typography"`.
Applications can register their own Go modules through `cli.Run`.
`Filesystem.LoadStylesheet` and `Filesystem.LoadModule` provide the same loaders
for library callers, including package CSS imports and relative asset URLs.

Watch mode polls for changes, keeps the last valid CSS after an error, and
avoids rewriting unchanged output. `--poll=100` sets the interval in
milliseconds; `--watch=always` keeps running after stdin closes.

Use `--map` for an inline source map, or `--map public/app.css.map` for a separate
file. Source maps include imported stylesheets and trace generated utilities
back to their definitions or `@apply` uses. Watch mode updates a changed map
without rewriting identical CSS.

Minification and the `canonicalize` command are still pending.
The CLI has not yet passed the full upstream CLI integration suite.

For source maps in Go, set `Config.From` to the entry stylesheet's filename,
then call `BuildWithSourceMap` on the compiler or an incremental builder.
It returns CSS and a `SourceMap`, which you can marshal with `encoding/json`.
`sourceMap.Inline()` returns a comment with an embedded map; `Comment(url)` links
to a separate file. `Visualize(css)` shows mappings beside the original source
for debugging. Leave `From` empty when you do not need source locations.


Reuse existing CSS
------------------

If your application already ships a stylesheet, add only the helpers it lacks:

```go
existing, err := rocketwind.DefinedClasses(mainCSS, widgetsCSS)
compiler := rocketwind.New(rocketwind.Config{ExistingClasses: existing})
css, err := compiler.Build(templateClasses)
```

Class names are read from CSS selectors, including escaped names and nested
rules. Text inside comments, declarations, attributes, `:not()` and `:has()`
does not count as a class definition. Exclusion applies to generated helpers;
`@apply` and named rules still resolve those utilities. Imported stylesheets
must be passed separately. Rocketwind does not compare declaration values:
when a class already exists, the supplied stylesheet owns its behavior.


Standard plugins
----------------

`@tailwindcss/forms` **0.5.11** is built in. Use `@plugin "@tailwindcss/forms"`
in a stylesheet, with the same `strategy: "base"` or `strategy: "class"` option,
or pass `rocketwind.Forms(rocketwind.FormsOptions{})` to `NewWithPlugins`.
Its CSS matches 24 differential cases against the real plugin, plus 20 SVG
encoding cases. This upstream release contains no automated tests to import.

`@tailwindcss/typography` **0.5.20** is also built in, including prose modifiers,
element variants, custom class names and the legacy selector option. In Go, use
`Typography(TypographyOptions{})`; `Styles` replaces its defaults and `Extend`
customizes selected declarations or selectors. All 16 original upstream tests
pass with their pinned Tailwind 3.2.2 dependency. The same cases plus four default
configurations match Tailwind 4.3.4 output; 20 selector cases also match.

The older **aspect-ratio 0.4.2**, **line-clamp 0.4.4** and **container-queries
0.1.1** plugins are also available, through their `@plugin` names or the
`AspectRatio`, `LineClamp` and `ContainerQueries` Go functions. Their options
accept ordered named values. Aspect-ratio supplies the older padding-based
layout. Modern Tailwind already includes line-clamp and container queries in
core, so new applications usually don't need those two plugins.

All six original tests for these three plugins pass with their legacy Tailwind
dependencies. Their inputs and 24 additional cases match Tailwind 4 output.
The line-clamp comparison supplies a no-op `variants()` function because its
JavaScript release still calls that API, which Tailwind 4 removed. The Go port
has no such dependency. Original legacy CSS results are retained for testing
the pending compatibility profile.


Tailwind compatibility
----------------------

| Version | Status |
| --- | --- |
| Tailwind CSS **4.3.4** | Current target. All 14,396 captured upstream calls pass, covering compiler output, errors, syntax, normalization, CSS nesting, configuration, source extraction, filesystem scanning, URL rewriting and source maps. The full upstream suite is not yet ported, so complete compatibility is not yet verified. |
| Tailwind CSS **3.4.17** | Planned compatibility profile for existing applications. Not yet implemented or verified. |

The goal is to reproduce the core compiler and standard plugins in Go, including
their upstream tests. Running JavaScript configuration or arbitrary JavaScript
plugins is outside the scope. Those extensions need Go implementations.

Version compatibility includes defaults and generated CSS, not just accepting
the same class names. An older application must be able to keep its existing
styles while adopting Rocketwind. New templates should be able to use the
current version. Utilities already supplied by another stylesheet must not be
generated twice.

The library currently has **zero dependencies**. Node, Rust and ICU are used
only to run upstream tests and generate reference data during development.
The Go compiler does not run external tools.
